claims.text: The studied alloy is equiatomic, Co-free FeNiCrMn, corresponding to approximately 25 at.% of each element.
Conventional solidification of equiatomic FeNiCrMn yields a predominantly single-phase FCC microstructure.
The dynamic mechanical behavior of solidified equiatomic FeNiCrMn is governed by competition between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Low temperature and high strain rate shift FeNiCrMn toward twin-dominated deformation.
Deformation twinning produces localized strain heterogeneities in FeNiCrMn.
Deformation twinning manifests as abrupt changes in grain orientation.
Twin boundaries impede subsequent dislocation movement and thereby increase strain hardening.
Twin-enhanced strain hardening preserves the strength–ductility balance of FeNiCrMn under low-temperature or high-rate loading.
At higher temperatures and lower strain rates, FeNiCrMn deforms predominantly by thermally activated dislocation slip.
Reduced thermal activation under low-temperature or high-rate conditions favors deformation-twin nucleation over dislocation motion.
Local strain-field evolution, twin formation, and grain-orientation changes mediate the macroscopic dynamic response.
DIC strain hotspots will spatially correlate with regions in which EBSD identifies deformation twins.
In-situ TEM will show greater deformation-twin density and activity at low temperatures and high strain rates.
In-situ TEM will show slip-dominated deformation at high temperatures and low strain rates.
Twin density will correlate with the measured mechanical response across the temperature and strain-rate matrix.
Quasi-static room-temperature deformation of FeNiCrMn is predominantly controlled by dislocation slip.
The strain-rate and temperature thresholds for the slip-to-twinning transition can depend on processing and microstructural state.
The study will compare tensile and compressive loading at 77 K, 300 K, and 500 K over strain rates from about 10^-3 to 10^2–10^3 s^-1.
The hypothesis is restricted to solidified, single-phase FCC FeNiCrMn and is not asserted for defect-rich or multiphase variants.

A failure to observe increased twinning and associated strain heterogeneity under low-temperature, high-rate loading, or a failure of mechanical response to correlate with a slip-to-twinning transition, would falsify the hypothesis.
